keyConcepts.title: The Internet is a network of networks
keyConcepts.text: End systems (hosts) connect through access ISPs, which connect to regional ISPs and tier-1 ISPs. IXPs, peering and content provider networks tie them together.

keyConcepts.title: Protocols define communication
keyConcepts.text: A protocol sets the format and order of messages exchanged and the actions taken when a message is sent or received. TCP and IP are the Internet's core protocols.

keyConcepts.title: Edge vs. core
keyConcepts.text: The **edge** is hosts and access networks (DSL, cable, fiber, WiFi, cellular). The **core** is the mesh of routers and links that moves packets between them.

keyConcepts.title: Packet switching vs. circuit switching
keyConcepts.text: Packet switching shares link capacity on demand and suits bursty traffic. Circuit switching reserves capacity end-to-end (FDM or TDM), which wastes it when users are idle.

keyConcepts.title: Store-and-forward
keyConcepts.text: A router must receive a whole packet before forwarding it. Over N links of rate R, one packet of L bits takes **N·L/R** seconds.

keyConcepts.title: The four delays
keyConcepts.text: Nodal delay = processing + queuing + transmission (**L/R**, depends on packet size) + propagation (**d/s**, depends on distance).

keyConcepts.title: Traffic intensity and throughput
keyConcepts.text: Keep traffic intensity **La/R** below 1, or queues grow without limit. End-to-end throughput is set by the slowest (bottleneck) link: **min(R1, …, RN)**.

keyConcepts.title: Five-layer stack and encapsulation
keyConcepts.text: Application (messages), transport (segments), network (datagrams), link (frames), physical (bits). Each layer adds its own header as data goes down the stack.

keyConcepts.title: Networks under attack
keyConcepts.text: Malware and botnets, DoS/DDoS attacks (vulnerability, bandwidth flooding, connection flooding), packet sniffing and IP spoofing.

flashcards.back: A device at the edge of the network that runs applications, such as a laptop, phone or server.
Rules defining the format and order of messages exchanged between entities, and the actions taken on sending or receiving a message.
The network that physically connects an end system to the first (edge) router on its path, e.g. DSL, cable, FTTH, WiFi or cellular.
**L/R**: packet length (bits) divided by link rate (bits/sec). Depends on packet size, not distance.
**d/s**: link length divided by propagation speed (about 2–3×10^8 m/s). Depends on distance, not packet size.
Packets arriving at a router faster than the outgoing link can send them, so they wait in the output buffer.
**La/R** (arrival rate × packet size ÷ link rate). If it's above 1, the queue grows without bound.
When a packet arrives at a router whose buffer (queue) is already full, so it gets dropped.
The slowest link on a path. It limits end-to-end throughput: throughput = min(R1, R2, …, RN).
**N·L/R** for one packet (ignoring other delays). For P packets: (N + P − 1)·L/R.
FDM gives each circuit its own frequency band all the time. TDM gives each circuit a fixed time slot in every frame.

flashcards.front: The five Internet layers (top to bottom)
flashcards.back: Application, Transport, Network, Link, Physical.
Message (application), segment (transport), datagram (network), frame (link), bits (physical).
Each layer adds its own header to the data from the layer above, e.g. a segment becomes the payload of a datagram.
Layers 1–3 (physical, link, network). Link-layer switches implement layers 1–2. Hosts implement all five.
An Internet exchange point: a meeting point where many ISPs peer (exchange traffic) with each other.
A virus needs user interaction to spread (e.g. opening an attachment). A worm spreads with no user interaction.
A distributed denial-of-service attack: many sources (often a botnet) flood a target so legitimate users can't use it.
Sending packets with a false source IP address. Defended against with end-point authentication.

flashcards.front: Who created the Web, and when did ARPAnet switch to TCP/IP?
flashcards.back: Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web at CERN. ARPAnet switched to TCP/IP on January 1, 1983.

quiz.q: Which delay depends on the distance between two routers?
quiz.explain: Propagation delay is d/s: the link's length divided by the signal's speed. Transmission delay (L/R) depends on packet size, not distance.

quiz.q: A 1,000-bit packet is sent on a 1 Mbps link. What is the transmission delay?
A packet of L bits crosses 3 links, each of rate R, using store-and-forward. Ignoring other delays, how long does it take?
quiz.explain: Each of the N = 3 links must receive the whole packet before forwarding it, so the delay is N·L/R = 3L/R.

quiz.q: What happens when traffic intensity La/R is greater than 1?
options: The queue grows without bound and delay approaches infinity
quiz.explain: Bits arrive faster than they can be sent, so the queue keeps growing. Systems must be designed so traffic intensity stays below 1.

quiz.q: A path has links of 10 Mbps, 2 Mbps and 100 Mbps. What is the end-to-end throughput?
quiz.explain: Throughput is limited by the bottleneck (slowest) link: min(10, 2, 100) = 2 Mbps.

quiz.q: Which layer moves datagrams from one host to another across the network?
quiz.explain: The network layer (IP) moves datagrams host to host. The transport layer works process to process; the link layer works one hop at a time.

quiz.q: What is a packet called at the transport layer?
Why is packet switching better than circuit switching for bursty traffic?
options: It shares link capacity on demand, so more users can share a link
It guarantees a constant rate to every user
quiz.explain: Users are rarely all active at once, so sharing capacity on demand supports many more users. Circuit switching wastes reserved capacity during silent periods.

quiz.q: Which access technology is a shared broadcast medium, so neighbors can slow each other down?
quiz.explain: In cable internet, homes in a neighborhood share the same downstream channel, so speed can drop when many people are online.

quiz.q: Which layers does a typical router implement?
quiz.explain: Routers work up to layer 3 (network). Link-layer switches implement layers 1–2, and hosts implement all five.

quiz.q: What does a packet sniffer do?
options: Passively records copies of packets passing by
Sends packets with a fake source address
quiz.explain: Sniffers passively capture traffic, which makes them hard to detect. Encryption is the main defense.

quiz.q: Which statement about the OSI model is true?
options: It has seven layers, including presentation and session
It has five layers, like the Internet stack
quiz.explain: OSI adds presentation and session layers. The Internet stack leaves those functions to applications.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an IXP?
options: A meeting point where multiple ISPs peer with each other
A device that converts DSL to cable
A server that stores web pages
quiz.explain: Internet exchange points let ISPs connect and exchange traffic directly (peering) instead of paying a provider.

quiz.q: Which type of malware spreads without any user interaction?
quiz.explain: Worms exploit vulnerable network apps to spread on their own; viruses need a user to do something, like open an attachment.
